'''George Berzsenyi''' ({{IPA|hu|ˈbɛrʒɛɲi}}; August 17, 1938 – June 4, 2026) was a Hungarian-American mathematician and professor, known for his contributions to mathematics education and his mentorship of high-school mathematics students. He founded and chaired the [[American Invitational Mathematics Examination]] (AIME), founded the [[United States of America Mathematical Talent Search]] (USAMTS), and helped create several other problem-solving programs for mathematically gifted students. For his contributions, he received the [[Paul Erdős Award]] in 1996 and the [[Yueh-Gin Gung and Dr. Charles Y. Hu Award for Distinguished Service to Mathematics|Gung and Hu Award]] in 2016.<ref name="MAAaward">{{cite web |title=Yueh-Gin Gung and Dr. Charles Y. Hu Award for Distinguished Service to Mathematics |url=https://maa.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/JMM_2016_Prize_Booklet_complete.pdf#page=57 |publisher=Mathematical Association of America |date=January 7, 2016 |access-date=June 29, 2026 |pages=55–58}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Berzsenyi was born in [[Budapest]], Hungary, on August 17, 1938, as György de Vargha. Both parents came from old Hungarian nobility. His mother Kornélia descended from the poet [[Dániel Berzsenyi]]. György and his father, Colonel Miklós de Vargha, were among the many thousands who emigrated to the United States in 1957 after Soviet troops crushed the [[Hungarian Revolution of 1956]].<ref name=Childhood/><ref>{{cite report |url=https://archives.nato.int/report-on-hungarian-refugees-note-by-the-chairman-of-the-committee-of-political-advisers |title=Report on Hungarian Refugees |last=Casardi |first=A. |publisher=NATO |date=April 17, 1957 |access-date=August 1, 2026 |id=C-M(57)65 |pages=12–13 |quote=The United States offered asylum to 30,000 Hungarian refugees; this quota will be filled by the end of March 1957.}}</ref>

György soon officially changed his name to George Berzsenyi.<ref name=Childhood>{{cite web |title=György (George) Berzsenyi's Hungarian Childhood Homes |url=https://www.childhoodhomestories.com/post/gy%C3%B6rgy-george-berzsenyi-s-hungarian-childhood-homes |website=Childhood Home Stories |date=June 27, 2024 |access-date=May 16, 2025}}</ref> He earned his doctorate in mathematics from [[Texas Christian University]] in 1969,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.mathgenealogy.org/id.php?id=8855 |title=George Berzsenyi |work=Mathematics Genealogy Project |access-date=June 27, 2026}}</ref> with a specialization in [[complex analysis]].<ref>{{cite web |title=George Berzsenyi Author Page |url=https://www.amazon.com/George-Berzsenyi/e/B0997GQQM4 |website=Amazon.com |date=2021 |access-date=May 16, 2025}}</ref>

==Academic career==
Berzsenyi taught mathematics at [[Lamar University]] in Beaumont, Texas, for 19 years.<ref name="StEdwardsARML">{{cite web |title=The Story of ARML in Texas |url=https://edwarde.create.stedwards.edu/ARML.html |website=St. Edward's University |access-date=May 16, 2025}}</ref> He later joined [[Rose–Hulman Institute of Technology]] (RHIT) in Terre Haute, Indiana, where he continued to teach and promote mathematics enrichment for 12 years<ref name="StEdwardsARML" /> until his retirement in 1999.

==Competitions and outreach==

===Mathematics Day and Texas Mathematical Olympiad===
At Lamar University, Berzsenyi organized an annual "Mathematics Day" (1977–1982) for high-school students. He also created the Texas Mathematical Olympiad during this period.<ref name="MAAaward"/>

===In-person coaching===
Berzsenyi was the first coach of the Texas team for the [[American Regions Mathematics League]] (ARML) in 1980.<ref name="StEdwardsARML"/> He also mentored students for the Westinghouse/Intel [[Science Talent Search]] and similar competitions.<ref name="MAAaward"/>

===AIME and AMC involvement===
{{main|American Invitational Mathematics Examination}}
In 1983, Berzsenyi became the founding chair of the [[American Invitational Mathematics Examination]] (AIME) committee and served for six years. He also contributed problems to the [[American Mathematics Competitions]] (AMC), including the earlier American High School Mathematics Examination (AHSME).<ref name="MAAaward"/> These annual exams have been the primary selectors of students for the [[USA Mathematical Olympiad]], leading in turn to the [[International Mathematical Olympiad]].

===USAMTS and IMTS===
{{main|United States of America Mathematical Talent Search}}
In 1989, Berzsenyi founded the [[USA Mathematical Talent Search]] (USAMTS), a nationwide proof-based contest by mail. Modeled on Hungary's ''[[Középiskolai Matematikai Lapok]]'' (''KöMaL''), it provided high-school students with extended time and personalized feedback for their work. Berzsenyi directed the contest through the 1990s, and later co-edited problem sets for the International Mathematical Talent Search (IMTS).<ref>{{cite web |title=Mathematical Work – George Berzsenyi |url=https://www.berzsenyifamily.net/copy-of-mathematical |website=BerzsenyiFamily.net |access-date=May 16, 2025}}</ref> For much of the 1990s, he invited 30 of the strongest USAMTS solvers to spend three weeks at the [[National Science Foundation|NSF]]-funded Young Scholars Program at RHIT, where they studied various topics from classical geometry to chaos theory.

===The Competition Corner===
Berzsenyi edited "The Competition Corner" in ''The Mathematics Student'' from 1978 until the journal ended in 1981. This was the first of his Hungarian-style proof-by-mail efforts (eventually becoming USAMTS) that helped develop hundreds of American high-school mathematicians through year-round creative problem-solving.<ref name="MAAaward"/>

==Death and legacy==
Berzsenyi died June 4, 2026, at the age of 87. He was survived by his wife Kay after 61 years of marriage, and by their children and grandchildren.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://obituaries.tribstar.com/obituary/george-berzsenyi-1093869587 |title=Dr. George Berzsenyi Obituary |work=[[Tribune-Star]] |location=Terre Haute |date=June 27, 2026 |access-date=July 29, 2026}}</ref>

His mathematical protégés include numerous academics and scientists. Among them are [[Noam Elkies]], [[Kiran Kedlaya]], and [[Vamsi Mootha]], who credited Berzsenyi's mentorship in an [[NPR]] feature.<ref>{{cite news |last=Palca |first=Joe |title=A Math Teacher's Life Summed Up By The Gifted Students He Mentored |url=https://www.npr.org/2019/04/07/707326070/a-math-teachers-life-summed-up-by-the-gifted-students-he-mentored |work=NPR |date=April 7, 2019 |access-date=May 16, 2025}}</ref>

==Recognition==
In 1996, Berzsenyi received the [[Paul Erdős Award]] from the [[World Federation of National Mathematics Competitions]] for his contributions to national competitions and educational enrichment.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.wfnmc.org/erdberzenyi.html |title=George Berzsenyi: Paul Erdős Award |publisher=World Federation of National Mathematics Competitions |date=July 1996 |access-date=July 2, 2026}}</ref> In 2016, he received the [[Gung and Hu Award]] from the [[Mathematical Association of America]] for a lifetime of distinguished service.<ref name="MAAaward"/>
